stem: Where does a C# program start running?
options: The first line of the file
explanation: The runtime looks for a method called Main and starts there. With top-level statements the compiler writes Main for you, but it still exists.

stem: What does every C# statement end with?
explanation: Statements end with a semicolon. New lines and indentation mean nothing to the compiler - they are purely for humans.

AB then C on a new line
explanation: Write prints without a line break, so A, B and C all land on one line. Only WriteLine moves to a new line - after printing C.

stem: Why does console.WriteLine("hi"); fail to compile?
options: C# is case sensitive - it is Console
explanation: C# is case sensitive: console and Console are different names. The class is Console with a capital C.

stem: What does 'using System;' at the top of a file do?
options: Lets you write Console instead of System.Console
explanation: System is a namespace full of built-in types. The using directive means you can refer to them by their short names.

stem: What does the C# compiler produce from your source code?
explanation: The compiler produces IL, a CPU-independent bytecode. The JIT compiler turns that into real machine code when the program runs - which is why one .dll runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

stem: What does this print when score is 10?
explanation: The semicolon straight after the if ENDS the if statement - it guards an empty statement. The block below is not attached to the if, so it always runs. A classic bug.

stem: Which of these is a valid single-line comment?
explanation: C# uses // for single-line comments and /* */ for blocks. # is Python; <!-- --> is HTML.

stem: What groups statements together into a block in C#?
explanation: Braces group statements, exactly where GCSE pseudocode used ENDIF or ENDWHILE. Indentation is only for human readers - unlike Python.

stem: A file contains just: Console.WriteLine("hi"); Is this a valid program?
options: Yes - the compiler wraps it in Main for you
explanation: Since C# 9, top-level statements are allowed in one file. The compiler generates the class and Main around them - the long form still exists underneath.
